items.title: Dedekind domains
Localizing a Dedekind domain at a nonzero prime gives a DVR
items.strategy: Unpack the Dedekind hypotheses, observe that a nonzero prime in a one-dimensional domain has height one, and invoke the published height-one localization theorem.

items.title: Local DVRs at the nonzero primes force global normality
items.strategy: At the zero prime the localization is the fraction field; at every nonzero prime the hypothesis gives a DVR, hence an integrally closed local domain. Apply the published local-normality criterion.

items.title: Local DVRs at the nonzero primes force dimension one
items.strategy: Localize at a nonzero prime. The hypothesis makes the localization a DVR, so its only primes are zero and the maximal ideal; the localization-prime correspondence then forces every nonzero prime of the original domain to be maximal, unless the ring is already a field.

items.title: Equivalent local characterizations of Dedekind domains
items.strategy: One direction localizes a Dedekind domain at each nonzero prime. Conversely, use the preceding normality and dimension lemmas to recover the global definition; the locally principal clause comes from the DVR ideal theorem after localizing each nonzero proper ideal.

items.title: A localization of a Dedekind domain is Dedekind or a field
items.strategy: Noetherianity and integral closure localize. Prime correspondence shows every surviving nonzero prime is still maximal, and if no nonzero prime survives then the localization is a field.

items.title: The trace pairing in a finite separable extension is nondegenerate
items.strategy: Specialize the published trace-form theorem to the bilinear pairing (x,y) maps to Tr(xy).

items.title: Finite separable integral closures over normal Noetherian domains are module-finite
items.strategy: Choose a fraction-field basis together with a trace-dual basis. For an integral element, its traces against the chosen basis lie in the base ring, so the integral closure embeds in a finite trace-dual lattice and is therefore a finite module.

items.title: The integral closure of a Dedekind domain in a finite separable extension is Dedekind
items.strategy: Use module-finiteness from the previous theorem, retain normality by construction, and apply the local Dedekind characterization to the localizations above nonzero primes.

items.title: Why the finite-separable hypothesis is retained in the integral-closure theorem
Fractional ideals
Products, colons, and inverse candidates for fractional ideals
The basic operations on fractional ideals are well defined
items.strategy: Clear denominators simultaneously for sums, products, colons, and scalar multiples. Boundedness descends from the common multiple, and the fixed ambient fraction field makes independence of chosen presentations formal.

items.title: Invertible fractional ideals
Equivalent characterizations of invertible fractional ideals
items.strategy: If I times I inverse is the whole ring, a finite expression of 1 gives generators and a dual basis, proving finite projective rank one and local principality. Conversely, if the localizations are principal at every maximal ideal, then the quotient R over I times I inverse localizes to zero everywhere, so the product equals R.

items.title: Every nonzero fractional ideal of a Dedekind domain is invertible
items.strategy: Localize the given fractional ideal at each maximal ideal. In a DVR every nonzero fractional ideal is principal, so the local characterization of invertibility globalizes.

items.title: Prime-ideal valuations on fractional ideals
Prime-ideal valuations of a fractional ideal have finite support and add under products
items.strategy: A common numerator and denominator of the fractional ideal involve only finitely many prime divisors, so all other localizations are units. Additivity is immediate after localizing and reading exponents in the relevant DVR.

items.title: Unique factorization of nonzero fractional ideals into prime powers
items.strategy: Build the candidate product from the finitely many local exponents. The ideal and the candidate have the same localization at every nonzero prime, so the local criterion identifies them; uniqueness is equality of every prime valuation.

items.title: For Dedekind ideals, divisibility reverses inclusion
items.strategy: Compare the prime exponents in the unique factorization of the two ideals.

items.title: Every nonzero ideal in a Dedekind domain is generated by two elements
items.strategy: Fix a nonzero element a in the ideal. Choose a second element by simultaneous congruences so that the two-generated ideal has the same prime valuations as the original one, then compare valuations.

items.title: The ideal class group
The ideal class group quotient is well defined
items.strategy: Principal fractional ideals are closed under product and inverse, and replacing representatives by principal multiples changes the product by another principal factor. Thus multiplication descends to equivalence classes.

items.title: The divisor group of a Dedekind domain
The principal-divisor exact sequence for a Dedekind domain
items.strategy: Send a nonzero fraction to the finitely supported valuation vector of its principal ideal. Unique ideal factorization identifies the divisor group with all valuation vectors on fractional ideals, from which exactness at each term is read off.

items.title: A Dedekind domain is a PID exactly when its class group is trivial
items.strategy: If every class is trivial, every nonzero ideal differs from the unit ideal by a principal factor and is therefore principal. Conversely, in a PID every nonzero fractional ideal is principal, so the quotient group is trivial.

items.title: A finite rank-one projective module embeds as a fractional ideal
items.strategy: Tensor the finite projective module with the fraction field to get a one-dimensional vector space, choose a basis, and clear denominators of a finite generating set to realize the module inside the fraction field.

items.title: Invertible fractional ideals are exactly the rank-one projective modules
items.strategy: One direction is the local and projective criterion for invertible ideals. For the converse, embed a finite rank-one projective module as a fractional ideal and use the tensor-product evaluation pairing to identify that fractional ideal as invertible.

items.title: The ideal class group is the Picard group of rank-one projectives
items.strategy: Transport fractional-ideal multiplication to tensor product of rank-one projective modules via the previous theorem. Principal fractional ideals correspond to free rank-one modules, so the quotient is exactly the Picard group.

items.title: Finite torsion-free modules over Dedekind domains are projective
items.strategy: A finite torsion-free module injects into its fraction-field extension. After localizing at each maximal ideal of a Dedekind domain, it becomes a finitely generated torsion-free module over a DVR, hence free; the finite-projective criterion then globalizes.

items.title: A nonzero finite projective module over a Dedekind domain splits off a rank-one summand
items.strategy: Choose a nonzero fraction-field functional, clear denominators to obtain a surjection onto a fractional ideal, and split the map because both source and target are projective.

items.title: Finite torsion-free modules over Dedekind domains have Steinitz form
items.strategy: Induct on rank. Split off rank-one projective summands until only one remains, convert rank-one projectives to invertible ideals, and use the determinant or top exterior ideal to show that the final ideal class is independent of the chosen decomposition.

items.title: Submodules of projective modules over Dedekind domains are projective
items.strategy: A submodule of a projective module is torsion free. Its finitely generated submodules are projective by the finite Steinitz theory, and the hereditary Stacks devissage upgrades the directed union inside a projective ambient module; flatness then follows from projective implies flat, while arbitrary torsion-free modules are flat by the Dedekind local-DVR criterion.

title: Dedekind Domains and Ideal Classes — Examples

items.title: Every nonfield PID is a Dedekind domain with trivial class group
items.strategy: Use principality to get local principal ideals and Noetherianity, then apply the class-group characterization.

items.title: A semilocal Dedekind domain is a PID
items.strategy: For each maximal ideal choose an element vanishing there and unit elsewhere by the Chinese remainder theorem. This makes every maximal ideal principal, and then the class-group criterion finishes.

items.title: A fractional ideal of the integers with positive and negative prime exponents
items.strategy: Write the fractional ideal as a denominator multiple of an ordinary ideal, factor numerator and denominator into primes, and read off the signed exponent vector.

items.title: Computing an inverse fractional ideal explicitly
items.strategy: Compute the colon ideal by the divisibility condition in the fraction field, then multiply the two factorizations and compare valuations to verify the inverse relation.

items.title: A rank-two module and its Steinitz class
items.strategy: Take a module of the form R direct sum I, compute its determinant ideal class, and compare with the Steinitz classification theorem.

items.title: Localizing a Dedekind domain at a nonzero prime
items.strategy: Localize at a named nonzero prime, identify the surviving maximal ideal, and read the ideal exponents from the localized factorization.

items.title: Constructing two generators for a Dedekind ideal
items.strategy: Choose a nonzero element already in the ideal, pick a second element by the two-generator theorem's congruence conditions, and verify equality prime by prime.

items.title: The divisor and class of a fractional ideal
items.strategy: Translate the signed prime-ideal factorization into its divisor vector and then pass to the quotient by principal divisors.

items.title: A noninvertible ideal in a singular one-dimensional domain
items.strategy: Use a singular domain such as k[t^2,t^3] and the ideal generated by t^2 and t^3. Localizing at the singular maximal ideal shows it is not principal, so the Dedekind local criterion and the invertibility criterion both fail.
